newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN passes the mike on East Timor human rights woes.
newsitem.headline: UN passes the mike on East Timor human rights woes.

text.p: Behind-the-scenes politicking at the U.N. Human Rights Commission boiled down to one small but important decision on Thursday: which microphone would East Timor activist and Nobel laureate Jose Ramos Horta be allowed to use?

Horta's supporters had campaigned for him to address the body from the main microphone at the podium, like previous Nobel Peace prize laureates, former Archbishop Desmond Tutu of South Africa and Rigoberta Menchu, a Guatemala-born Maya Indian.
But Indonesia and its Asian allies, backed by the African group, blocked this, saying he should only be allowed to speak from the microphone reserved for non-governmental organisations.
Diplomats said negotiations on the terms of Horta's speech, its length, subject and his seat had yet to be concluded.
Chairman of the Commission, Miroslav Somol, said states had blocked Horta from taking the floor from the podium as a guest speaker: "Unfortunately, it is out of the question."

But the question of the use of the microphone was a very serious one, according to the Czech chairman: "It is a very sensitive issue for some delegations. So I think it's normal there are discussions and a lot of time spent on these issues."
About 2,000 officials and activisits are attending the forum which churned out 7,000 pages of official documents, translated, reproduced and distributed, at a cost of $9 million last year.
Horta, co-winner of 1996's Nobel peace prize and campaigner for self-determination on the disputed island, slammed the forum for failing to stand up to Indonesia and dictators.
"This Commission isn't exactly one that looks after human rights," said the exiled foreign minister of East Timor invaded by Indonesia in 1975 after Portugal withdrew from its ex-colony.

"The Human Rights Commission is increasingly discredited by actions of dictatorships. If countries do not stand up to dictators, the human rights machinery created in the past 50 years will be in jeopardy."

Horta urged the Commission to adopt a "strongly worded resolution" on rights abuses by Indonesia in East Timor, whose troops he accused of torture and arbitrary detention. He counted on support from European Union, the Unites States and Canada.
He said he would not address the Commission as scheduled on Thursday but hoped to be there later in its session in April.

Horta, who was awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize along with the Roman Catholic bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo, repeated his call for a U.N.-supervised referendum on the island on whether to choose independence or integration into Indonesia.

The international community does not recognise the Roman Catholic-dominated territory's annexation. Talks under U.N. auspices between Portugal and Indonesia, aimed at finding an internationally-acceptable solution, have dragged on since 1983.
Residents believe 200,000 people were killed during the invasion, a subsequent famine and over two decades of strife.
